reo.intro: Every passage and draft is written for practice; the writers, places and figures in them are invented.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-7 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay by a retired traffic engineer, published in the opinion section of a regional newspaper. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer and publication are invented.)

[1] Every weekday at a quarter past eight, Grace Adeyemi leaves the pharmacy on Caldwell Avenue with a paper bag in one hand and a cane in the other, and every weekday she does the same arithmetic. The walk signal at Caldwell and Fifth gives her eighteen seconds to cross five lanes. She needs about thirty. So she waits, sometimes through two or three cycles, for a gap in traffic long enough to make up the difference, and when the gap does not come, she crosses anyway, one hand raised toward the turning cars as if she could hold them back.

[2] I spent thirty-one years timing intersections like that one, and I would like to say I never timed one so badly. I cannot. The walking speed we plugged into our formulas came from a manual, and the manual's number described a brisk adult with nothing in her hands. It was not a cruel number. It was simply the number that let the most cars through.

[3] That is the part worth dwelling on. A signal runs on a fixed cycle, and every second granted to people on foot is a second taken from people in cars. When engineers assume a fast walker, the walk phase shrinks, the green light for traffic grows, and the intersection "performs," a word we used without irony, in the only column of the report anyone read: vehicle delay. Pedestrian delay had no column. Neither did the woman with the cane.

[4] The results are not hard to find. When the county studied its crash records last year, it found that residents over sixty-five made up about one in six of its population but nearly one in three of the pedestrians killed in its crosswalks. The report called the finding "notable." It is more than notable. It is what one should expect after decades of designing for a walker who does not exist and treating everyone slower than that walker as a rounding error.

[5] Some readers will object that longer walk signals would snarl traffic, and on a few of our busiest corridors they might add a minute to a commute. I do not dismiss that minute; I have sat in it. But when the city of Vellmont retimed forty of its intersections for slower walkers three years ago, the average rush-hour delay for drivers rose by less than eight seconds, and pedestrian injuries at those intersections fell by nearly half over the next two years.

[6] None of this requires new technology or a new line in the budget. It requires a different number, and a different idea of whom the number is for. An intersection is not a machine for moving cars that people on foot occasionally interrupt; it is a public place, and everyone who must cross it, whether driving, walking, or leaning on a cane, has an equal claim to reach the other side.

[7] The county should retime every signal within half a mile of a pharmacy, clinic, school, or senior center to the pace of the slowest people who regularly cross there, and it should do so before the next budget is written, not after. Mrs. Adeyemi has done her arithmetic every weekday for years. It is time the county did its own.

parts.q:
The writer does not state his recommendation until paragraph 7. Which of the following best explains how this arrangement serves his purpose with the newspaper's readers?
(A) It lets the writer present the county's crash data before he has to admit that he helped to cause the problem himself.
(B) It spares the writer from having to answer the objection that longer walk signals would slow down drivers.
(C) It leads readers from one walker, to the cause of her trouble, to its scale, so the proposal arrives as a conclusion.
(D) It reproduces the order in which the writer himself came to doubt the manual's walking speed during his career.
parts.a: (C). The essay moves from Mrs. Adeyemi's daily crossing (paragraph 1) to the cause, a walking speed chosen to move cars (paragraphs 2 and 3), to the scale of the harm in the county's records (paragraph 4), and only then, after answering an objection, to the recommendation. By paragraph 7 the proposal reads as the place the reasoning was already heading, which matters for newspaper readers, many of them drivers, who might resist a demand stated at the outset. (A) reverses the order: the writer's admission comes in paragraph 2, before the data in paragraph 4. (B) is contradicted by paragraph 5, which raises and answers exactly that objection. (D) confuses the essay's rhetorical order with a record of the writer's own thinking; nothing in the passage says he came to doubt the manual in this sequence.
parts.n: REO-1.A (a line of reasoning that arrives at a thesis), skill 5.A. Thinking: explain what a delayed thesis does for a particular audience. Trap: (D), which treats the order of an argument as a diary of how the writer reached it.

parts.q:
The writer's account of his own career in paragraph 2 contributes to the line of reasoning chiefly by
(A) tracing the problem to an accepted professional standard, not to careless engineers, which prepares for paragraph 3
(B) confessing his personal guilt so that readers will be more willing to forgive the engineers who still work for the county
(C) supplying evidence of how many of the county's intersections were timed using the manual's walking speed over the years
(D) turning the essay away from the present-day problem at Caldwell and Fifth toward a history of traffic engineering
parts.a: (A). 'It was not a cruel number. It was simply the number that let the most cars through' reflects on the writer's experience and draws its significance: the short signal is the product of a standard everyone followed, chosen to serve traffic. That diagnosis is exactly what paragraph 3 goes on to explain ('That is the part worth dwelling on'). (B) mistakes the admission for a plea; the writer asks nothing on behalf of other engineers, and the point of 'I cannot' is that the problem is built into the practice. (C) is wrong because the paragraph gives no count of intersections; its support is experience, not data. (D) overreads one paragraph: the writer turns at once to how signals work now and never traces the profession's history.
parts.n: REO-1.I (narration with reflection on its significance), skill 5.C. Thinking: ask what the narrated experience lets the next paragraph do. Trap: (B), which reads the confession as an emotional plea rather than as a step in the causal explanation.

parts.q:
In paragraph 3, the sentence 'Pedestrian delay had no column' functions in the writer's cause-effect reasoning as
(A) an effect of the fast walking speed, since shorter walk phases made the delay for people on foot too small to be worth recording
(B) part of the underlying cause, since a report that measured only drivers' delay made every shorter walk phase look like pure gain
(C) a concession that engineers had no reliable method for measuring how long people on foot wait to cross at an intersection
(D) evidence that the engineers knowingly ignored the manual's own instructions about how long the walk phase ought to be
parts.a: (B). The writer's chain runs: the report measured only vehicle delay, so assuming a fast walker, which shrinks the walk phase and lengthens the green, always improved the one number anyone read, and nothing on the page recorded what walkers lost. The missing column is therefore part of why the harmful choice kept being made, not a result of it. (A) reverses cause and effect: a short walk phase increases the wait for people on foot, and the column was missing regardless. (C) invents a measurement problem the paragraph never raises; the point is that no one looked, not that no one could. (D) contradicts paragraph 2, where the walking speed came from the manual itself.
parts.n: REO-1.J (cause-effect), skill 5.C. Thinking: place one sentence in a causal chain, distinguishing a cause from an effect. Trap: (A), which puts the missing column after the short signal rather than before it.

parts.q:
Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the conclusion the writer draws from the county's crash records in paragraph 4?
(A) The county's report was written by staff in the same department that sets the timing of the county's signals.
(B) Residents over sixty-five in the county walk fewer miles each week, on average, than younger residents do.
(C) The share of the county's residents who are over sixty-five has grown steadily over the past decade.
(D) Older pedestrians are far more likely than younger ones to die from injuries of the same severity.
parts.a: (D). The writer infers that older residents' share of deaths is 'what one should expect' from signals timed for fast walkers. If older pedestrians are more likely to die from the same injury, the gap could arise even if they were struck no more often than anyone else, so the figures would no longer point to signal timing as the cause. (A) invites suspicion of bias, but a department reporting a finding that reflects badly on its own work gives readers less reason to doubt the finding, not more. (B) would strengthen the point: if older residents walk less yet die at twice their share, their risk per trip is even higher. (C) describes a trend over time, but the finding compares shares measured at the same moment, so a growing older population does not explain the gap.
parts.n: REO-1.F (flaws that can make reasoning specious), skill 5.A. Thinking: find the alternative explanation that breaks the step from a pattern in the data to the writer's cause. Trap: (A), which treats any possible bias as a weakness without asking which way the bias would push.

parts.q:
Suppose the writer had placed paragraph 5 immediately after paragraph 1. Which of the following best describes the most likely effect on the argument?
(A) Readers would weigh a minute of delay against one woman's crossing, not against a cause and a county-wide harm not yet shown.
(B) The argument would grow more persuasive, because a writer should always answer the strongest objection before offering any evidence.
(C) The effect would be slight, because nothing in paragraph 5 depends on what paragraphs 2 through 4 have established.
(D) The essay would now state its thesis first, because paragraph 5 contains the writer's recommendation to the county.
parts.a: (A). Paragraph 5 asks readers to accept a small cost to drivers. That request is persuasive after paragraphs 2 through 4 have shown why the walk phase is short and that older residents die in the county's crosswalks at about twice their share. Moved up, the objection would be answered before any of that is known, and a minute of every commuter's time would be set against a single anecdote. (B) applies a rule no writer must follow; answering an objection before readers know what is at stake hands the objection the advantage. (C) is wrong because 'longer walk signals' makes sense only once paragraph 3 has explained the trade between the walk phase and the green light. (D) misreads paragraph 5, which answers an objection; the recommendation is in paragraph 7.
parts.n: REO-1.E (the sequence of paragraphs reveals the line of reasoning), skill 5.A. Thinking: test what a paragraph depends on by imagining it moved. Trap: (B), a rule of thumb applied without asking what the reader would know at that point.

parts.q:
In paragraph 4, the writer's response to the report's word 'notable' implies that the county's report
(A) exaggerated the danger to older pedestrians in order to win money for new signals
(B) was mistaken about the share of pedestrian deaths among residents over sixty-five
(C) recorded the gap as a curiosity without explaining it as the result of a design choice
(D) was written by engineers who did not know that people's walking speeds differ with age
parts.a: (C). 'It is more than notable' does not dispute the numbers; it rejects the report's treatment of them. The writer's commentary supplies what the report left out: the pattern is 'what one should expect' after decades of designing for a walker who does not exist. The report, he implies, noticed the gap and stopped short of its cause. (A) reverses the complaint: the writer thinks the report understated the finding's significance, not overstated it. (B) is wrong because the writer relies on the report's figures; he quarrels with its interpretation, not its data. (D) goes beyond the text: the passage says engineers used the manual's number, not that they were unaware that people walk at different speeds.
parts.n: REO-1.D (commentary explains the significance of evidence), skill 5.A. Thinking: infer what a writer's commentary says about someone else's failure to comment. Trap: (B), which takes a disagreement about meaning for a disagreement about the numbers.

parts.q:
A reader objects: 'Paragraph 6 says that everyone has an equal claim to cross an intersection, so limiting the longer signals in paragraph 7 to certain intersections is inconsistent.' Which of the following best evaluates the objection?
(A) The objection is sound, and the writer should have deleted paragraph 6 so that his recommendation would not contradict it.
(B) The objection misses that paragraph 7 applies the principle first where slow walkers cross most, which also answers paragraph 5.
(C) The objection is sound, because the passage gives no evidence that slow walkers ever cross near pharmacies or clinics.
(D) The objection is beside the point, because a conclusion is not expected to follow logically from the paragraphs that come before it.
parts.a: (B). Paragraph 6 argues about whom signal timing should serve; paragraph 7 puts that principle into practice where the walkers it describes cross most often, near pharmacies, clinics, schools, and senior centers. The limit also keeps the cost to drivers on the busiest corridors, the concern granted in paragraph 5, small. A priority is not a contradiction. (A) would delete the principle that justifies the recommendation. (C) overlooks paragraph 1: Mrs. Adeyemi's crossing begins at a pharmacy. (D) states a false rule; the essay's whole design depends on the conclusion following from what precedes it.
parts.n: REO-1.A (a line of reasoning that arrives at a thesis), skill 5.A. Thinking: judge whether a limited recommendation is consistent with the principle and the concession before it. Trap: (A), which treats any limit on a principle as a contradiction of it.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-14 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay by a professional baker, published in a magazine for home cooks. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer and publication are invented.)

(1) A recipe is not a set of instructions. (2) It is a record of someone else's judgment, written down in the hope that a stranger can borrow it. (3) Whether you can borrow it depends less on how exact the recipe is than on how much of that judgment it lets you see.

(4) Consider two recipes for the same sandwich loaf. (5) The first, copied onto an index card in my grandmother's hand, calls for "flour, enough," a rise "in a warm spot till doubled," and baking "until it knocks hollow." (6) The second, from a test kitchen that bakes each recipe forty times before printing it, calls for 500 grams of flour, a 90-minute rise at 75 degrees, and 35 minutes in a 375-degree oven.

(7) Judge them first by what they assume about the cook. (8) My grandmother's card assumes that you have stood beside her at the counter and know what "enough" feels like in your hands; the test kitchen's assumes only that you own a scale. (9) Now judge them by what they do when something changes. (10) On a humid July afternoon, when the flour has already drawn moisture from the air, dough made with exactly 500 grams turns out slack and sticky, while the card, which never promised a number, tells you to keep adding flour until the dough stops clinging to your fingers. (11) In a 60-degree kitchen in January, a 90-minute rise leaves a dense brick, while the card, which asks you to wait "till doubled," has never let the clock decide.

(12) So the precise recipe wins the first test and loses the second. (13) Its numbers are accurate, but they are accurate for one kitchen on one afternoon, and the recipe does not say so. (14) The judgment is still there, hidden inside the numbers: someone in that test kitchen watched the dough, pressed it, and wrote down what it happened to need that day. (15) Handed only the result of that watching, you never learn to watch.

(16) I do not mean that we should all bake from index cards. (17) A beginner handed "flour, enough" has nothing to go on, and my grandmother's card would have been useless to me at twelve, before she taught me what it meant. (18) A vague recipe is not wiser than a precise one; its wisdom has simply never been written down.

(19) The best recipes, then, do both jobs. (20) They give the number and the sign together: "about 500 grams, until the dough pulls away from the bowl"; "35 to 40 minutes, until the bottom sounds hollow when tapped." (21) The number gets a beginner started. (22) The sign teaches the beginner to stop needing the number. (23) A recipe written this way does what my grandmother did at the counter, which was to show me what she was looking at, and it is the only kind of recipe that can be trusted in a kitchen its writer has never seen.

parts.q:
In sentence 3 the writer claims that whether a recipe can be borrowed depends 'less on how exact the recipe is than on how much of that judgment it lets you see.' How do sentences 19-23 relate to that claim?
(A) They restate the claim in new words, adding nothing that sentences 1-3 had not already said about recipes.
(B) They abandon the claim, since after sentences 16-18 the writer decides that exact numbers matter most to cooks.
(C) They narrow the claim to beginners, since only beginners, the writer says, need to see the judgment in a recipe.
(D) They turn the claim into a standard for writing recipes: pair each number with the sign that shows the judgment.
parts.a: (D). The passage states its claim at the start and then justifies it; the final paragraph converts that claim into practice. If a recipe is usable to the extent that it shows its writer's judgment, the best recipe gives the number and also the sign the cook watches for ('until the dough pulls away from the bowl'), which is exactly what sentences 19-20 prescribe. (A) reflects the habit of treating every conclusion as a summary; the pairing of number and sign is new, and it depends on the concession in sentences 16-18. (B) misreads the concession: granting that a beginner needs numbers is not deciding that numbers matter most, and sentence 22 says the sign teaches the cook 'to stop needing the number.' (C) confuses who needs the number with who needs the judgment; sentence 21 says the number helps a beginner start, while the whole passage argues that every cook needs to see the judgment.
parts.n: REO-1.B (a claim stated first, then justified by a line of reasoning), skill 5.A. Thinking: trace how a conclusion develops, rather than repeats, a claim stated at the outset. Trap: (A), the reflex that a conclusion restates the thesis.

parts.q:
A student summarizes sentences 4-15 this way: 'The writer compares the two recipes and prefers her grandmother's because it is more personal, while the test kitchen's is merely more accurate.' Which of the following best evaluates the summary?
(A) It is accurate, since the writer's memory of learning at her grandmother's counter is her main reason for preferring the card.
(B) It is inaccurate, since the writer judges both recipes by the same two standards and finds that each one meets only one of them.
(C) It is inaccurate, since sentences 4-15 show the writer preferring the test kitchen's recipe because anyone can follow it.
(D) It is accurate in its verdict but not in its reasons, since the writer prefers the card because it is less exact, not more personal.
parts.a: (B). Sentences 7 and 9 set two like categories of comparison, what each recipe assumes about the cook and what each does when conditions change, and apply both to both recipes. Sentence 12 gives the verdict: the precise recipe 'wins the first test and loses the second.' The student's summary sets 'personal' against 'accurate,' two unlike categories the writer never uses, and invents a preference sentences 4-15 do not state. (A) takes the grandmother's counter, which returns only in sentence 23 as an image of the recommended recipe, for the basis of the comparison. (C) keeps only the first test and ignores sentences 10-11, where the precise recipe fails. (D) is half right, since the writer does not prize the card for being more personal, but it still assigns her an outright preference, and her objection to the precise recipe is that it hides its judgment, not that it is exact.
parts.n: REO-1.K (comparison-contrast uses like categories), skill 5.C. Thinking: judge a summary of a comparison by checking whether it keeps the writer's categories and verdict. Trap: (D), which corrects the reason but keeps the invented preference.

parts.q:
Sentences 1 and 2 define a recipe as 'a record of someone else's judgment' rather than 'a set of instructions.' This definition contributes to the passage's reasoning chiefly by
(A) establishing the writer's authority as a professional baker before she goes on to compare the two recipes
(B) conceding that no recipe can ever be followed exactly, a point that the writer later disputes in sentences 12-15
(C) setting the standard the rest of the passage uses: recipes are judged by how much of that judgment they reveal
(D) explaining a technical term that many readers of a magazine for home cooks might not already understand
parts.a: (C). By redefining a familiar object, the writer changes the question readers ask of it: not 'how exact is it?' but 'how much of its writer's judgment can I see?' That question drives the comparison (sentences 7-11), the verdict that the precise recipe hides its judgment 'inside the numbers' (sentence 14), and the recommendation (sentences 19-23). (A) is a true description of the byline, but sentences 1-2 say nothing about the writer's profession; the definition does its work through an idea, not a credential. (B) misreads the definition as a concession; the writer never grants that recipes cannot be followed, and sentences 12-15 extend the definition rather than dispute it. (D) treats a redefinition as a glossary entry; home cooks know what a recipe is, which is why the surprising definition does rhetorical work.
parts.n: REO-1.L (definition as a method of development), skill 5.C. Thinking: explain what a definition sets up for the rest of the argument. Trap: (D), which reads any definition as information for readers who lack a term.

parts.q:
The parallel wording of sentences 7 and 9 ('Judge them first by...' and 'Now judge them by...') helps the reader chiefly by
(A) marking two separate standards of comparison, which sentence 12 then refers to as 'the first test' and 'the second'
(B) signaling that the two recipes turn out to be more alike than the opening of the passage had led readers to expect
(C) showing that the writer judges her grandmother's card more strictly than she judges the test kitchen's recipe
(D) introducing the objections to the writer's claim that she goes on to answer in sentences 16 through 18
parts.a: (A). The repeated imperative 'judge them... by' tells the reader that sentence 9 begins a second category of comparison parallel to the first, so the two tests can be held side by side. Sentence 12 depends on that structure: 'the first test' and 'the second' make sense only because the parallel wording set them up. (B) reverses the effect; the two standards are the means of showing how differently the recipes behave. (C) is unsupported, since both recipes are held to the same two standards and each passes one. (D) confuses the standards of comparison with objections; sentences 16-18 are a concession about beginners, which neither sentence 7 nor sentence 9 anticipates.
parts.n: REO-1.O (parallel structure develops a relationship between elements), skill 5.B. Thinking: explain how a repeated structure lets a later sentence refer back to it. Trap: (D), which assumes any sentence that begins a new move introduces a counterargument.

parts.q:
If sentences 16-18 were deleted, which of the following would most likely happen to the passage's line of reasoning?
(A) Little would change, because sentences 16-18 only repeat the point about beginners that sentence 21 makes.
(B) The comparison would lose its second standard, because sentences 16-18 explain what happens when conditions change.
(C) The passage would lose its thesis, because sentence 18 states the main claim more directly than any other sentence.
(D) The passage would seem to side with the card, and sentence 21's reason for keeping the numbers would lack support.
parts.a: (D). After sentences 12-15 fault the precise recipe, a reader would expect the writer to recommend the index card. Sentences 16-18 block that conclusion by granting what the card lacks ('A beginner handed "flour, enough" has nothing to go on'), and that concession is why the final paragraph keeps the number: sentence 21 ('The number gets a beginner started') rests on it. Without it, 'The best recipes, then, do both jobs' would arrive without the step that justifies 'both.' (A) is half right, since sentence 21 does echo sentence 17, but sentence 21 is the conclusion drawn from that point, not a substitute for it. (B) misplaces the second standard, which is set in sentence 9 and applied in sentences 10-11. (C) mistakes a qualifying sentence for the thesis; the claim is stated in sentences 1-3 and turned into a recommendation in sentences 19-23.
parts.n: REO-1.E (the sequence of paragraphs reveals the line of reasoning), skill 5.A. Thinking: predict what a later paragraph loses when the step it depends on is removed. Trap: (A), which sees the overlap with sentence 21 but not that sentence 21 depends on it.

parts.q:
Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the writer's reasoning in sentences 13-15?
(A) Cooks who bake only from recipes with exact numbers learn to adjust for weather as often as cooks whose recipes give signs.
(B) Test kitchens bake each recipe forty times in the same kitchen, under the same conditions, before they print the recipe.
(C) Many index-card recipes handed down in families leave out whole steps of the method as well as the exact amounts.
(D) Most readers of magazines for home cooks own a kitchen scale and weigh their flour rather than measuring it by the cup.
parts.a: (A). Sentences 13-15 are commentary that draws a consequence from the comparison: a recipe that gives only numbers hides the judgment behind them, so its user 'never learn[s] to watch.' If cooks who use number-only recipes learn to adjust as often as cooks whose recipes give signs, the hidden judgment does not keep them from learning, and the step from sentences 10-11 to sentence 15 fails. (B) would strengthen the reasoning, since testing in one kitchen under fixed conditions is exactly why the numbers are 'accurate for one kitchen on one afternoon.' (C) describes a weakness of the index card, which the writer has already granted in sentences 16-18, so it does not touch sentences 13-15. (D) bears on the assumption named in sentence 8, that the precise recipe requires only a scale, and says nothing about whether its numbers teach judgment.
parts.n: REO-1.C (commentary connects evidence to a claim), skill 5.A. Thinking: find the fact that breaks the link between the evidence and the consequence the writer draws from it. Trap: (C), which attacks the index card, a weakness the writer has already conceded.

parts.q:
Which of the following is most closely analogous to the kind of recipe the writer recommends in sentences 19-23?
(A) A trail guide that drops every distance in favor of landmarks, so that hikers learn to read the trail for themselves
(B) A trail guide whose distances were measured by satellite on forty separate hikes over the same route in one season
(C) A trail guide that gives the distance to each turn and describes the landmark, such as a split boulder, that marks it
(D) A trail guide that advises hikers to walk the route once with an experienced ranger before they attempt it alone
parts.a: (C). The writer recommends giving 'the number and the sign together': a quantity that gets a beginner started and a thing to watch for that teaches the beginner to stop needing the quantity. A distance paired with a landmark does both jobs. (A) is the index card in another setting, all signs and no numbers, which sentences 16-18 reject for beginners. (B) is the test kitchen's recipe, numbers made precise by repetition under one set of conditions, which sentences 13-15 fault. (D) is tempting because sentence 23 mentions the grandmother's lessons at the counter, but the writer's point is that the best recipe does on the page what she did in person, so a guide that sends the hiker to a person instead is not the analogue.
parts.n: REO-1.B (a claim developed and justified), skill 5.A. Thinking: carry the writer's recommendation into an unfamiliar context. Trap: (D), which matches the image in sentence 23 instead of the recommendation it illustrates.

mc.stem:
Questions 15-20 refer to the following.

The following two letters were published a week apart in the letters section of a town's weekly newspaper while the town council was deciding whether to repair the town's outdoor pool or replace it with a splash pad, a paved play area with fountains and sprinklers but no standing water. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writers, the town, and the figures are invented.)

Letter 1

[1] Last July, a nine-year-old boy slipped into the deep end of the Linden Street Pool and had to be pulled out by a lifeguard, coughing and frightened. Since then I have not let my own children swim there, and I am not alone: attendance at the pool fell sharply in August. The lesson is plain. The pool is no longer safe.

[2] The council now faces a simple choice. It can spend 1.2 million dollars to repair a sixty-year-old pool, or it can build a splash pad for about a third of that. A splash pad has no deep end, needs no lifeguards, and has never drowned anyone. Ridgemont built one three years ago, and families there say they love it.

[3] Some will say that a splash pad is no place to swim laps or to learn to swim. But children today can take lessons at the YMCA, and teenagers have more to do than they did when the pool was built. We cannot let nostalgia for the pool's past put our children in danger.

Letter 2

[1] Last week's letter read the rescue at Linden Street as proof that the pool is dangerous. I read it as proof that the pool works. I was a lifeguard there for six summers, and I know what happened that afternoon: a boy lost his footing where the floor slopes toward the deep end, and a guard reached him in under ten seconds, because that is what guards are trained and paid to do. A pool where no one ever gets into trouble does not exist. A pool where someone is watching when they do is what the town's lifeguard budget buys.

[2] Nor did the rescue empty the pool. August visits fall every year, when football practice starts and families leave on vacation. Here are the parks department's own figures:
Summer · July visits · August visits
2021 · 4,100 · 2,900
2022 · 4,300 · 3,100
2023 · 3,900 · 2,800
2024 · 4,200 · 3,000
2025 · 4,000 · 2,600
The rescue kept no one away. Last August was an ordinary August.

[3] It is true that a splash pad would cost about a third as much to build. But compare what each would give the town for its money. A splash pad serves children young enough to be happy running through a sprinkler; the pool serves everyone from toddlers to the retirees who swim laps at six in the morning. A splash pad teaches no one anything; last summer the pool's free lessons taught 330 children to swim. The YMCA's lessons cost 90 dollars a child and are a twenty-minute drive away, which puts them out of reach of the families who most need free ones. A town that cannot swim is not made safer by removing the water it learns in.

[4] Repair the pool.

parts.q:
In paragraph 1 of Letter 1, the writer concludes that 'the pool is no longer safe.' Which of the following best identifies the most serious flaw in the reasoning that leads to this conclusion?
(A) The writer relies on a single personal anecdote, and an anecdote cannot serve as evidence in a written argument.
(B) The writer never names the boy or the lifeguard, so readers have no way to confirm that the rescue took place.
(C) The one event cited, a boy pulled out by a lifeguard, could as easily show that the pool's safeguards work.
(D) The writer's own children stopped swimming at the pool, so the writer has seen nothing of the pool since the rescue.
parts.a: (C). The writer moves from one incident to a general verdict, but the incident ended with a lifeguard pulling the boy out, which is what a safe, supervised pool is designed to do. The evidence does not point toward the conclusion rather than its opposite, and Letter 2 builds its reply on exactly this reading. (A) overcorrects: an anecdote can be legitimate evidence, and the problem is what this one shows, not that it is an anecdote. (B) raises a question of verification that no reader of a local letter would need settled; the rescue is not in dispute, only its meaning. (D) is a weak objection, since the conclusion rests on the rescue and the August attendance, not on what the writer has seen at the pool since.
parts.n: REO-1.F (flaws that make reasoning specious), skill 5.A. Thinking: test whether the evidence supports the conclusion better than it supports the opposite. Trap: (A), the belief that personal anecdotes are never valid evidence.

parts.q:
Both letters open by narrating the same rescue. Which of the following best describes the difference in how the two writers use that narration?
(A) Letter 1 narrates the rescue in more detail than Letter 2, which mentions it only in passing before it turns to figures.
(B) Letter 1 tells the story from a parent's point of view, while Letter 2 tells it from the point of view of the boy himself.
(C) Letter 1 treats the rescue as evidence about the pool's staff, while Letter 2 treats it as evidence about the pool's design.
(D) Letter 1 takes the event as a sign of danger and moves at once to a verdict; Letter 2 adds details and reflects on them.
parts.a: (D). Letter 1 gives the event in one sentence and draws its conclusion three sentences later. Letter 2 supplies the details that matter to its reading, where the boy fell, how fast the guard reached him, and that this is what guards are 'trained and paid to do,' and then reflects on their significance: 'A pool where someone is watching when they do is what the town's lifeguard budget buys.' Narration serves Letter 2's reasoning because the writer draws an insight from it. (A) reverses the two; Letter 2's account is the longer and more specific. (B) is wrong because Letter 2 narrates from a lifeguard's knowledge, not from the boy's point of view. (C) seizes on the detail about the sloping floor, but Letter 2 uses that detail to explain how the boy fell, not to argue about the pool's design, and Letter 1 never discusses the staff.
parts.n: REO-1.I (narration offers details and reflects on their significance), skill 5.C. Thinking: compare how two writers turn one event into evidence. Trap: (C), which takes a descriptive detail for the point of the paragraph.

parts.q:
The writer of Letter 2 concludes from the table that 'the rescue kept no one away' and that 'last August was an ordinary August.' Which of the following best evaluates that conclusion?
(A) The table supports only part of it: August visits fall every year, but the drop last August was the steepest of the five.
(B) The table supports it fully, since August visits fell in every one of the five summers, including those before the rescue.
(C) The table undercuts it, since July visits in the summer of the rescue were lower than in any earlier summer shown.
(D) The table cannot bear on it, since the figures give visits for whole months rather than for the days after the rescue.
parts.a: (A). In 2021-2024, August visits ran about 71 to 72 percent of July's (2,900 of 4,100; 3,100 of 4,300; 2,800 of 3,900; 3,000 of 4,200). In 2025 they were 2,600 of 4,000, or 65 percent, the steepest drop and the lowest August in the table. The figures do show that an August decline is normal, which undercuts Letter 1's use of it, but they do not show that last August was ordinary or that the rescue kept no one away; Letter 2's commentary claims more than its evidence shows. (B) is the half of the reading the writer wants, and it ignores the size of last year's drop. (C) misreads the table: July 2025 (4,000) was higher than July 2023 (3,900). (D) is too dismissive, since monthly totals across five years are exactly the comparison needed to test whether last August was unusual.
parts.n: REO-1.D (commentary explains the significance of evidence), skill 5.A. Thinking: compute the pattern in the table and judge whether the writer's commentary claims more than the figures show. Trap: (B), which checks the direction of the drop but not its size.

parts.q:
Suppose the writer of Letter 2 had ended paragraph 3 after the sentence about the 330 children. Which of the following best describes the most likely effect?
(A) The paragraph would lose its evidence, since the figures about swimming lessons appear only in the sentences that were cut.
(B) The paragraph would still show what the pool offers, but it would no longer answer Letter 1 on the YMCA or on danger.
(C) The paragraph would grow more persuasive, since commentary distracts readers from the facts that carry the argument.
(D) The paragraph would change very little, since readers can be trusted to connect the lessons to children's safety themselves.
parts.a: (B). The sentences that would be cut are the paragraph's commentary. The YMCA sentence answers Letter 1's claim that children 'can take lessons at the YMCA,' and the last sentence turns the evidence about lessons against Letter 1's central charge, that the pool puts children 'in danger.' Without them the paragraph would still compare the two options, but it would not explain how that comparison bears on the council's question. (A) misplaces the evidence: the 330 children appear in the sentence that would remain. (C) reflects the belief that facts speak for themselves; here, uncut facts would leave Letter 1's safety argument standing. (D) makes the same assumption more politely; a writer who leaves the connection to readers leaves them free to draw Letter 1's.
parts.n: REO-1.M (a body paragraph's commentary explains how it contributes to the argument), skill 5.A. Thinking: predict what a paragraph loses when its commentary is cut. Trap: (D), the assumption that readers will supply the link themselves.

parts.q:
Paragraph 3 of Letter 2 responds to paragraph 2 of Letter 1 chiefly by
(A) disputing Letter 1's figures for the repair and offering the parks department's own estimate of the cost
(B) conceding that a splash pad is the better choice for young children while arguing that older swimmers need a pool
(C) granting Letter 1's comparison of cost, then comparing the two options on whom they serve and what they teach
(D) shifting the debate from the pool's safety to its long history, which Letter 1 had dismissed as mere nostalgia
parts.a: (C). Letter 1 compares the options on a single category, cost. Letter 2 accepts that comparison ('It is true that a splash pad would cost about a third as much') and then adds like categories, applied to both options: whom each serves (small children against everyone 'from toddlers to the retirees') and what each teaches (nothing against 330 children taught to swim). The added categories are the ones on which the pool wins. (A) invents a dispute; Letter 2 never questions the cost figures. (B) misreads the contrast, since Letter 2 says the pool also serves toddlers and concedes nothing about young children. (D) is wrong because paragraph 3 never mentions the pool's history; its last sentence returns to safety, the ground Letter 1 chose.
parts.n: REO-1.K (comparison-contrast with like categories), skill 5.C. Thinking: see how a reply keeps an opponent's category and adds others. Trap: (B), which reads the splash pad's audience as a concession.

parts.q:
The council wants to know which letter gives the more accurate picture of the pool's safety. Which of the following would best help it decide?
(A) A survey asking families in Ridgemont how much they enjoy their splash pad and how often they visit it each summer
(B) The age and swimming ability of the boy who was pulled from the deep end of the pool last July, as the lifeguard recorded them
(C) The number of teenagers in the town who have summer activities other than swimming available to them nearby
(D) The pool's record of serious injuries per thousand visits over many summers, compared with that of similar guarded pools
parts.a: (D). The letters disagree about what one rescue shows. A rate of serious injuries over many summers, compared with similar pools that have lifeguards, measures the thing in dispute: if the pool's rate is typical or low, Letter 2's reading holds; if it is high, Letter 1's does. Using a rate per thousand visits also corrects for how busy the pool is. (A) is Letter 1's own evidence about popularity; it says nothing about whether the pool is safe. (B) would add detail to the single incident, but a single incident is the problem with the evidence, not the solution. (C) bears on Letter 1's paragraph 3 about teenagers, not on safety.
parts.n: REO-1.F (flaws in a line of reasoning), skill 5.A. Thinking: design the evidence that would settle a dispute built on one incident. Trap: (B), which asks for more about the one case rather than for a pattern across many.

mc.stem:
Questions 21-25 refer to the following.

The following passage is a draft of a letter that a high school junior is writing to the director of transportation for her school district. The blank in sentence 6 marks a word or phrase the writer has not yet chosen. (Written for practice; the writer, the districts, and the figures are invented.)

(1) On winter mornings, the students who ride Bus 14 wait at the corner of Orchard Road and Pine Street for as long as twenty-five minutes, because no one can tell them when the bus will come. (2) I am writing to ask the district to put GPS trackers on its buses and to let families see where each bus is on a free app.

(3) Tracking would give students back the time they now spend waiting. (4) Right now, the only way to be sure of catching the bus is to arrive early and wait. (5) For six weeks last winter I kept a log of Bus 14's arrivals, and the bus came anywhere from four minutes early to twenty-one minutes late. (6) ______ a student who reaches the stop on time can wait twenty minutes, and a student who arrives two minutes late may already have missed the bus.

(7) The Carver Valley district added trackers to its forty buses two years ago. (8) The trackers cost about 150 dollars per bus, plus a small monthly fee. (9) In the first year, the district's transportation office received 60 percent fewer calls from parents asking where a bus was. (10) Tracking would also help your own office.

(11) Some parents may worry that an app would let strangers follow a school bus. (12) Carver Valley's app shows a bus's location only to families who sign in with a student's ID number, and it stops showing the bus once the last student has gotten off.

(13) Tracking would also make students safer. (14) A student who knows the bus is ten minutes away can wait indoors instead of standing at the side of the road in the dark.

(15) I hope the district will try tracking on its five longest routes next fall.

parts.q:
The writer wants to fill the blank at the beginning of sentence 6 (reproduced below) with a transition that shows how sentence 6 relates to the evidence in sentence 5.
'______ a student who reaches the stop on time can wait twenty minutes, and a student who arrives two minutes late may already have missed the bus.'
Which of the following best accomplishes this goal?
(A) In other words,
(B) Even so,
(C) Instead,
(D) Similarly,
parts.a: (A). Sentence 5 reports a range, from four minutes early to twenty-one minutes late; sentence 6 translates that range into what it means for a student standing at the stop, which is a restatement of the evidence in human terms. 'In other words' names that relationship and ties the log back to the claim in sentence 3. A reader who hears sentence 6 as a consequence of the range ('so') is reading the same link, the range's meaning for the student; none of the other choices offers a consequence, and each names a relationship that is plainly false here. (B) 'Even so' signals that sentence 6 holds true despite sentence 5, but the waits and missed buses happen because of the range, not in spite of it. (C) 'Instead' signals a replacement, as if sentence 6 described what happens in place of the arrivals in sentence 5. (D) 'Similarly' presents sentence 6 as a second, parallel point, when it is the meaning of the first.
parts.n: REO-1.Q (a transition indicates how evidence relates to the ideas around it), skill 6.B. Thinking: name the relationship between the evidence and the sentence that interprets it, then choose the word that states it. Trap: (B), chosen by students who hear a contrast between 'on time' and 'wait twenty minutes.'

parts.q:
The writer wants the director to know, before reading about Carver Valley, what that district's experience is evidence of. Which of the following revisions best achieves this goal?
(A) Delete sentence 10, since sentences 7-9 make its point clear enough without it.
(B) Move sentence 10 so that it opens the paragraph, coming before sentence 7.
(C) Move sentence 10 so that it follows sentence 3, joining the claim about time.
(D) Leave sentence 10 at the end, where it sums up what sentences 7-9 have shown.
parts.a: (B). Sentence 10 is the paragraph's claim, and sentences 7-9 are its evidence. Placed first, it tells the director what to look for in the Carver Valley figures, so the drop in parents' calls reads as proof that tracking helps the director's office rather than as a fact whose point arrives only afterward. (A) would leave the director to infer the claim, which the stated goal rules out. (C) would move the claim away from the only evidence that supports it and attach it to a paragraph about students' time. (D) is a legitimate arrangement for a paragraph that builds to its point, but it does not meet this goal, because the reader would reach the claim only after reading the evidence.
parts.n: REO-1.M (a body paragraph makes a claim and supports it with evidence), skill 6.A. Thinking: match the order of claim and evidence to a stated goal. Trap: (D), which defends the current order on general grounds instead of testing it against the goal.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that explains what the drop in parents' calls would mean for the director's own office. Which of the following best accomplishes this goal?
(A) Carver Valley's forty buses cover a district of about the same size as ours, so its results are likely to apply here.
(B) Each of those calls takes a dispatcher away from routing buses, so fewer calls would give your office back hours each week.
(C) Many parents in our district have told me that they would check such an app every morning if one existed.
(D) Clearly, Carver Valley made a wise decision when it chose to spend its money on trackers for all of its buses.
parts.a: (B). Commentary explains the significance of evidence for this reader. A 60 percent drop in calls matters to a director of transportation because each call costs a dispatcher's time; the sentence draws that consequence and applies it to the director's office, which also makes sentence 10's claim concrete. (A) is useful, since it argues that Carver Valley's results should carry over, but it defends the evidence's relevance without saying what fewer calls would mean for the office. (C) adds a new piece of evidence about demand rather than explaining the evidence already given. (D) is commentary in form only: it judges Carver Valley's decision without saying what the fewer calls would mean for this district.
parts.n: REO-1.C (commentary connects evidence to the claim), skill 6.A. Thinking: tell commentary that explains significance apart from new evidence and from an unexplained verdict. Trap: (A), which strengthens the evidence without explaining it.

parts.q:
The writer wants the concern raised in sentence 11 to come immediately after the reason it most directly challenges. Where should sentences 11 and 12 be placed?
(A) Where they are now, after sentence 10
(B) Before sentence 3, right after the request
(C) After sentence 14, following the safety paragraph
(D) After sentence 6, following the paragraph on waiting
parts.a: (C). The worry that strangers could follow a school bus is a worry about safety: it suggests that tracking could make students less safe, the reverse of the claim in sentence 13. Placed after sentence 14, the concern answers that reason directly, and sentence 12's reply lets the letter move straight to its request in sentence 15. (A) keeps the concern after the paragraph about the transportation office, a reason it does not touch. (B) raises an objection before the reader has heard any reason for tracking. (D) attaches the concern to the paragraph on waiting time, which it does not challenge.
parts.n: REO-1.N (coherence: the ideas in one paragraph link to the next), skill 6.B. Thinking: identify which reason an objection answers and place the two together. Trap: (A), which leaves the concern where it sits because it already follows most of the reasons, without asking which reason it answers.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that it ties the safety reason back to the scene in sentence 1 while keeping its point about how tracking makes a student safer. Which of the following best accomplishes this goal?
(A) Like the students at Orchard and Pine, a student anywhere in the district could then wait somewhere warm and dry.
(B) Across the district, students wait at more than two hundred stops, many on roads without sidewalks or streetlights.
(C) The students of Bus 14, like students everywhere, deserve to know that the district takes their safety seriously.
(D) A student who knows Bus 14 is ten minutes away can wait indoors instead of standing at Orchard and Pine in the dark.
parts.a: (D). Repeating 'Bus 14' and 'Orchard and Pine' links the sentence to the opening, so the reader pictures the same students at the same corner, and the sentence keeps the mechanism by which tracking makes them safer: knowing when the bus will come, a student can wait indoors rather than by the road in the dark. (A) recalls the corner but trades safety for comfort ('warm and dry'), so the reason no longer supports sentence 13. (B) adds evidence about danger across the district but makes no link to sentence 1. (C) recalls Bus 14 and names safety, but it drops the explanation of how tracking makes anyone safer and replaces it with a general appeal.
parts.n: REO-1.O (repetition links elements of a text), skill 6.B. Thinking: meet a two-part goal, checking that the repetition links back without losing the reason's substance. Trap: (C), which repeats a key term and names safety but loses the explanation.

fr.title: Argument: do we come to value only what we count?
fr.stem:
In a book about how organizations make decisions, a management consultant wrote: 'An organization comes to value only what it measures. Whatever it does not count, it soon stops seeing.' (The consultant and the book are invented for practice.)

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which the consultant's claim is valid.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rows.earns: A defensible position on the extent to which organizations come to value only what they measure, for example: 'Measuring does narrow what an organization pays attention to, as a school that ranks itself by test scores or a restaurant that times every table shows, but the consultant is wrong that the uncounted is lost for good: counting is usually also how an organization learns to see again, once someone starts measuring what it missed.' Agreeing, disagreeing, or qualifying the claim by condition (what kind of organization, what kind of measure) can all earn the point, and the thesis may take more than one sentence.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('organizations value what they measure'); 'measurement has advantages and disadvantages' with no position on the claim; an obvious fact ('businesses keep track of numbers'); or a summary of the consultant's statement.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how. Evidence may come from school (a class where participation is graded by the number of comments, so students talk more and listen less), sports (a team that tracks points but not the passes that set them up), work (a call center timed on call length, which rewards hanging up), public life (a traffic study that measured drivers' delay and not walkers'), or personal experience (a step counter that turned a walk into a number). Each is followed by commentary on what the measure made people attend to, what dropped from sight, and why, or, in a counterexample, how counting something new restored what had been ignored. The paragraphs are ordered so each builds on the last.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for each claim, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it ('this shows that measuring matters'), or the paragraphs could be shuffled with no loss because no line of reasoning joins them. 1: mostly general evidence ('in today's world everything is about numbers') and summary. 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. Three examples of 'bad metrics' that each end with the same sentence repeat the thesis rather than advance it.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently explores a tension, for example that measurement both blinds and reveals, so the remedy for a bad count is usually a better count joined to judgment rather than no counting at all; or distinguishing what cannot be counted (trust, a student's curiosity) from what simply has not been counted yet, and following the difference through the essay; or articulating the implication for how a school or city should choose its measures; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: 'Of course, numbers are also useful' added to the conclusion; a counterexample raised once and dropped; or a sweeping closing claim about society and data. The complexity must shape the argument throughout, not decorate its last paragraph.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that takes a defensible position on the consultant's claim and previews a line of reasoning.
parts.a: Model: 'The consultant is right that a measure quietly becomes a goal, so that a school graded on test scores teaches to the test and a clinic judged by how fast it sees patients shortens the visits; but the claim is wrong in its second half, because the neglected thing usually comes back into view the same way it left, when someone counts it.' It takes a position, qualifies it at a stated point, and previews two steps of reasoning (how measures narrow attention; how new measures restore it).
parts.n: 'Measuring things can be good or bad depending on the situation' names both sides without taking a position or saying which situations, and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with specific evidence and the commentary that explains how it supports your claim.
parts.a:
¶1 A measure becomes the goal: a class that grades participation by counting comments. Commentary: students learn to talk often rather than well, and the teacher who wanted discussion gets a stream of short remarks; the number was meant to show engagement and ends up replacing it, which is the consultant's first sentence at work.
¶2 What drops from sight: a traffic study that recorded drivers' delay and not walkers'. Commentary: no one decided that walkers did not matter, but a report with no column for them made every decision that cost them look free, so the harm grew unseen for years; this is the consultant's second sentence, and it shows the danger is not the counting but the counting of only one thing.
¶3 The limit of the claim: the same county saw the harm only when it counted crashes by age. Commentary: the uncounted was not lost for good; it returned once someone measured it, so the lesson is not to distrust counting but to ask, of every measure, who it leaves out. Building on ¶2, the problem and its remedy turn out to be the same tool used with different questions.
parts.n: Three paragraphs that each say 'this shows numbers can be misleading' earn at most 2; each paragraph needs its own step, placed so it depends on the one before.

parts.q: Row C plan: explain how this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Carry the tension that measurement both blinds and reveals through every paragraph: the participation count hides listening, the traffic report hides walkers, and in each case the essay asks what a second measure, or a person's judgment, would restore. The essay then argues that the consultant describes a habit of organizations rather than a law, one that a better choice of measures can break.
parts.n: Ending with 'in the future, artificial intelligence will measure even more of our lives' gestures at a broader context without explaining its implications, and earns nothing.

fr.title: Close reading: the crosswalk essay's concession and its evidence
fr.stem:
The paragraphs below are from the essay by a retired traffic engineer in questions 1-7. Reread them and answer the questions that follow. (Written for practice; the writer and publication are invented.)

[1] Every weekday at a quarter past eight, Grace Adeyemi leaves the pharmacy on Caldwell Avenue with a paper bag in one hand and a cane in the other, and every weekday she does the same arithmetic. The walk signal at Caldwell and Fifth gives her eighteen seconds to cross five lanes. She needs about thirty. So she waits, sometimes through two or three cycles, for a gap in traffic long enough to make up the difference, and when the gap does not come, she crosses anyway, one hand raised toward the turning cars as if she could hold them back.

[5] Some readers will object that longer walk signals would snarl traffic, and on a few of our busiest corridors they might add a minute to a commute. I do not dismiss that minute; I have sat in it. But when the city of Vellmont retimed forty of its intersections for slower walkers three years ago, the average rush-hour delay for drivers rose by less than eight seconds, and pedestrian injuries at those intersections fell by nearly half over the next two years.

[7] The county should retime every signal within half a mile of a pharmacy, clinic, school, or senior center to the pace of the slowest people who regularly cross there, and it should do so before the next budget is written, not after. Mrs. Adeyemi has done her arithmetic every weekday for years. It is time the county did its own.

parts.q: In paragraph 5 the writer grants that longer signals 'might add a minute to a commute' and adds, 'I do not dismiss that minute; I have sat in it.' Explain how this concession serves the writer's purpose with the newspaper's readers.
parts.a: The concession wins a hearing from the readers most likely to resist, drivers. By granting the cost before they can raise it, and by placing himself among them ('I have sat in it'), the writer shows he has weighed their interest rather than ignored it. That earns trust for the evidence that follows at once: in Vellmont the delay was under eight seconds, not a minute, while injuries fell by nearly half. The concession therefore shrinks the objection by measuring it instead of denying it, so a driver can accept the proposal without feeling dismissed.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the concession builds ethos' or 'shows the writer is fair' with no link to the drivers among the readers or to the Vellmont figures that follow; or the confident misreading that the writer agrees longer signals would snarl traffic and gives up that point.

parts.q: A student writes: 'The Vellmont evidence proves that if the county retimes its signals, pedestrian injuries at those intersections will fall by half.' Evaluate the student's claim, explaining what the evidence can and cannot show.
parts.a: The claim goes further than the evidence. Vellmont's result makes the proposal plausible and shows that the cost to drivers can be small, which is how the writer uses it. It cannot prove the same result in the county: it is one city, forty intersections, and two years; the county's traffic, crossings, and walkers may differ; and injuries at the retimed intersections may have fallen partly for other reasons, such as other changes made at the same time, or because the city chose intersections that had had an unusually bad stretch, which tend to improve on their own. A fair statement is that the evidence supports expecting fewer injuries, not a particular amount.
parts.n: Earns nothing: agreeing that the evidence proves a fifty percent drop because 'injuries fell by nearly half'; or a vague 'statistics can be misleading' that names no specific reason the Vellmont result might not transfer to the county.

parts.q: The essay begins and ends with Mrs. Adeyemi's 'arithmetic.' Explain how the final sentence's return to that word contributes to the essay's line of reasoning and to its purpose.
parts.a: In paragraph 1 the arithmetic is hers: eighteen seconds against the thirty she needs, a private calculation she must make because the signal did not. By paragraph 7 the essay has shown that the county's own arithmetic, a walking speed chosen to move the most cars, caused her problem. 'It is time the county did its own' turns the opening anecdote into the essay's demand: the county should redo its calculation with her in it. The repetition frames the essay, which gives it coherence, and it moves the burden from the woman to the county, which gives the recommendation its urgency.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'it brings the essay full circle' or 'it ends with emotion' without explaining how the meaning of 'arithmetic' has changed between paragraph 1 and paragraph 7.

fr.title: Commentary: turning a list of facts into a line of reasoning
fr.stem:
The following paragraph is from a student's draft of an argument essay on whether the town of Alder Creek should plant trees along its residential streets. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the student, the town, and the figures are invented.)

(1) Alder Creek should plant trees along every residential street. (2) A study by the Alder Creek Parks Department found that on summer afternoons, blocks with full tree cover were up to nine degrees cooler than blocks with no trees. (3) My grandmother's street has six old maples. (4) Planting a street tree costs the town about 300 dollars. (5) During last July's heat wave, the county's emergency rooms treated 212 people for heat illness. (6) Trees are also beautiful and make people happy.

parts.q: Explain why this paragraph, although each of its sentences may be accurate, does not yet develop a line of reasoning in support of sentence 1.
parts.a: The paragraph lists evidence without commentary, so the reader has to supply every link. Sentences 2 and 5 could work together, since cooler blocks bear on heat illness, but no sentence connects them or ties them to the claim; sentence 3 is an anecdote with no stated point; sentence 4 gives a cost that counts against the claim unless it is weighed against a benefit; and sentence 6 opens a new, unsupported claim. Because nothing explains how one piece leads to the next or to sentence 1, the sentences could be shuffled with no loss, which is the sign that there is no line of reasoning.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the paragraph needs more evidence' (it has plenty; what it lacks is commentary); or 'it is disorganized' without explaining what is missing between the pieces of evidence and the claim.

parts.q: Write two or three sentences of commentary, to follow sentence 5, that explain how sentences 2 and 5 together support the claim in sentence 1.
parts.a: Model: 'Those nine degrees are not a matter of comfort. In a July when 212 people in our county needed emergency care for heat, the hottest blocks are where the danger is greatest, and a tree that cools a street every afternoon protects the people on it before they ever need a doctor. At about 300 dollars a tree, that protection is one the town can afford to build street by street.' The commentary earns the point because it links the cooler blocks (sentence 2) to the heat illness (sentence 5) and both to the claim, and it turns the cost in sentence 4 from an objection into support.
parts.n: Earns nothing: commentary that restates ('This shows that trees are good for Alder Creek'); or sentences that add new evidence, such as another statistic, without explaining how sentences 2 and 5 connect to the claim.

parts.q: A classmate suggests opening the paragraph with sentence 5 instead of sentence 1. Would this change strengthen the paragraph? Justify your answer by predicting how the new order would shape a reader's understanding of it.
parts.a: Either answer earns the point with a justified prediction. Yes: opening with 212 people treated for heat illness presents the problem first, so if sentence 1 follows at once, the claim reads as the solution and the cooling study as the reason the solution works, a problem-to-solution order that gives the paragraph urgency. No: in the body of an argument essay the reader needs the claim first to know why a count of emergency room visits matters; opening with it could make the paragraph seem to be about hospitals, and the claim would arrive as an afterthought. The strongest answers note that the change helps only if commentary links the figure to the claim.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'yes, because a statistic is a good hook' or 'no, because the topic sentence always goes first,' neither of which predicts how the new order would change what the reader understands.

stl.intro: Every passage and draft is written for practice; the writers, places and figures in them are invented.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-7 refer to the following.

The following passage is a column published in a city newspaper shortly after the school district adopted a pacing calendar, which sets the date by which every class must finish each unit. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the newspaper, and the district are invented.)

(1) The district's new pacing calendar has been called rigid, and I would like to defend it by pointing out that it does not go nearly far enough. (2) The calendar tells each teacher which unit to finish by which Friday; it does not yet address the chief obstacle to finishing anything on time, which is the student who raises a hand.

(3) Consider the costs. (4) A single question from a single ninth grader ("Wait, why does that work?") can consume four minutes of instruction, and four minutes, multiplied across thirty students and a hundred and eighty days, is a loss no calendar can absorb. (5) Worse, questions are contagious. (6) One student asks why; a second, emboldened, asks what would happen if; by the third question, the class has wandered entirely off the calendar and into the subject.

(7) I therefore propose a modest fee: a nickel per question, payable in advance. (8) The fee would be low enough that no child is prevented from asking and high enough that every child would think twice, which is, after all, what we have always wanted children to do. (9) Questions about logistics ("Which page?") would be free. (10) Questions beginning with "why" would cost a dime, since they so rarely have short answers, and questions beginning with "what if" would be banned outright, as not one of them has ever been answered within a single class period.

(11) The benefits are easy to picture. (12) Lessons would end on the minute. (13) Units would close on their assigned Fridays. (14) Teachers, relieved of the burden of discovering what their students do not understand, could devote themselves entirely to the calendar. (15) And students would learn a valuable lesson about the cost of time, if about nothing else.

(16) I recognize that some parents will object to charging children for their curiosity. (17) To them I say only that the calendar is already charging it. (18) Every teacher in this district now knows exactly how many days she has left for fractions, and every teacher now has to decide, each time a hand goes up, whether the question in it is worth falling behind. (19) My fee is a nickel. (20) The calendar's fee is the question itself, and it is paid by the child who, having learned what questions cost, stops asking them.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the writer's actual position?
(A) The writer supports the calendar and wants it strengthened with a fee that would keep every class on schedule.
(B) The writer opposes the calendar, because by penalizing delay it discourages the questions through which students learn.
(C) The writer accepts the calendar but opposes the fee, which would fall hardest on families who could not afford it.
(D) The writer has no settled view of the calendar and asks parents to weigh its costs and benefits for themselves.
parts.a: (B). The proposal is ironic: the writer 'defends' the calendar by pushing its logic to an absurd fee, and sentences 17-20 drop the pose to say what the writer objects to. The calendar already makes teachers weigh each question against falling behind, and its cost is 'paid by the child who... stops asking.' (A) takes the proposal at face value and misses its cues, such as the ban on 'what if' questions and sentence 15's 'if about nothing else.' (C) treats the fee as a real proposal the writer might oppose, but the writer invented the fee, and the only thing sentences 16-20 criticize is the calendar. (D) mistakes the column's indirection for neutrality; sentence 20 states a clear judgment.
parts.n: STL-1.R (irony emerges from the gap between an argument and readers' values), skill 7.A. Thinking: infer a writer's real position from an ironic surface and the point where the irony drops. Trap: (C), which half-sees the irony but still treats the fee as the thing under debate.

parts.q:
In sentence 6, placing the phrase 'and into the subject' at the very end of the sentence chiefly serves to
(A) show that the writer regards students' questions as a distraction from the unit that the class is supposed to be covering
(B) complete the series of questions begun earlier in the sentence, so that the three students' questions are balanced
(C) signal a shift from the ironic tone of the column to the plain, sincere tone of the column's final paragraph
(D) reveal, in the sentence's last words, that what the calendar treats as a detour is the learning itself
parts.a: (D). The sentence builds as if describing a class losing its way ('wandered entirely off the calendar') and then ends where a reader expects a word like 'off topic' with 'into the subject.' The final position gives the twist its force: questions lead students into the subject the calendar is supposed to serve. (A) reads the sentence literally, as the column's pretended voice would; the end placement undercuts that view. (B) misdescribes the structure: the series of students ends with 'by the third question,' and the final phrase is not a fourth item but the turn. (C) misplaces the shift, which comes in sentence 17; sentence 6 is still in the ironic voice, and the joke works inside it.
parts.n: STL-1.L (the arrangement of words in a sentence can emphasize ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: explain what the end position of a phrase does to the meaning of the whole sentence. Trap: (A), the literal reading the irony is built to overturn.

parts.q:
In sentence 14, the phrase 'relieved of the burden of discovering what their students do not understand' contributes to the column's irony chiefly by
(A) suggesting that teachers already find the work of discovering what students do not understand a tiresome chore
(B) using technical terms from education research that the newspaper's general readers would not recognize
(C) describing the center of a teacher's work in words usually reserved for a hardship someone is glad to escape
(D) conceding that the calendar would give teachers more time, a benefit the writer takes seriously in sentence 18
parts.a: (C). 'Relieved of the burden' is the language of rescue from a hardship. Attaching it to 'discovering what their students do not understand,' which is what teaching is, exposes the proposal's values: a calendar that frees teachers from teaching. (A) attributes the pretended attitude to teachers; nothing in the column says they find the work tiresome, and the irony depends on readers knowing they do not. (B) mistakes plain words for jargon; the phrase is ordinary, which is why the mismatch is easy to hear. (D) misreads sentence 18, which says teachers must now weigh each question against falling behind; that is a cost, not a benefit.
parts.n: STL-1.A (connotation), with STL-1.R, skill 7.A. Thinking: explain how the connotation of a phrase clashes with what it describes. Trap: (A), which assigns the column's pretended attitude to the people it describes.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the change in tone that begins in sentence 17?
(A) From mock-earnest to plainly serious, as the writer drops the pretense of the proposal and names what the calendar costs
(B) From amused to bitter, as the writer gives up on persuading readers and turns instead to criticizing the district's teachers
(C) From sincere to sarcastic, as the writer abandons a practical proposal and begins to mock the parents who object to it
(D) From confident to uncertain, as the writer admits that the proposed fee might cost students more than the calendar does
parts.a: (A). Through sentence 16 the writer speaks as a straight-faced advocate of the fee. Sentence 17 ('the calendar is already charging it') drops the pose, and sentences 18-20 speak plainly about teachers weighing each raised hand and the child who 'stops asking.' The shift reveals the column's real target. (B) misreads the teachers in sentence 18 as the target; the writer presents them as constrained by the calendar, not at fault. (C) reverses the direction: the column moves from ironic to sincere, and the parents of sentence 16 are answered, not mocked. (D) inverts sentences 19-20, which set a trivial nickel against the calendar's far larger cost; the writer does not doubt which is greater.
parts.n: STL-1.F (a shift in tone can signal a qualification or reconsideration of perspective), skill 7.A. Thinking: name the direction of a tone shift and what it reveals about the writer's perspective. Trap: (C), which gets the direction of the shift backward.

parts.q:
A reader responds in a letter to the newspaper: 'Charging children a nickel to ask a question is cruel, and I am shocked that the paper printed this proposal.' Which of the following best evaluates the reader's response?
(A) The reader is right, since the writer admits in sentence 16 that parents will object to charging children for curiosity.
(B) The reader is wrong, since a nickel is small enough that, as sentence 8 says, no child would be prevented from asking.
(C) The reader takes the proposal literally, missing cues such as the ban on 'what if' and sentence 20's turn against the calendar.
(D) The reader's response is fair, since a satirical column is obliged to state its real position plainly in its very first sentence.
parts.a: (C). The column's exaggerations (a dime for 'why,' a ban on 'what if' because such questions are never answered in one period, students learning about time 'if about nothing else') signal that the proposal is not meant seriously, and sentences 17-20 say plainly that the cruelty the reader objects to is the calendar's. The reader shares the writer's values and has mistaken the target. (A) treats sentence 16 as an admission, but it sets up the reply that the calendar already charges the fee. (B) argues inside the ironic frame, defending a proposal the writer never meant. (D) states a rule satire does not follow; irony works by withholding the real position, and this column reveals it only at the end.
parts.n: STL-1.E (readers infer tone from word choice), with STL-1.R, skill 7.A. Thinking: judge a reader's response by the cues that should have signaled irony. Trap: (B), which answers the reader on the proposal's own terms.

parts.q:
The parallel clauses in sentence 8 ('low enough that no child is prevented from asking and high enough that every child would think twice') contribute to the column's irony chiefly by
(A) showing that the writer has weighed the interests of students and teachers and found them to be exactly equal
(B) giving the fee the balanced sound of a sensible compromise, which masks what the fee is designed to discourage
(C) placing more weight on the second clause than on the first, which reveals that the fee is meant to silence children
(D) introducing the list of free and costly questions in sentences 9-10, so that readers can see how the fee would work
parts.a: (B). The coordinated clauses 'low enough... and high enough' mimic the even-handed language of a policy compromise, so the fee sounds reasonable. Only the sentence's last clause, which treats 'think twice' (hesitate) as though it meant thinking, lets readers hear that the fee exists to make children hesitate to ask. (A) takes the balance as the writer's sincere judgment; the clauses weigh a child's asking against a child's hesitating, not students against teachers. (C) misreads coordination, which gives the two clauses equal weight; the irony comes from the balance, not from tipping it. (D) describes what follows the sentence, not what the parallel clauses themselves do.
parts.n: STL-1.J (coordination shows balance between ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: explain how a balanced structure lends false reasonableness to an absurd idea. Trap: (C), which expects the second of two coordinate clauses to carry more weight.

parts.q:
A student argues that sentences 19 and 20 are unnecessary, since sentence 17 has already stated the writer's point. Which of the following best evaluates this argument?
(A) The student is right, since a column should end as soon as its central point has been stated, and sentence 17 states it.
